title: The emperor on the langar floor
hookLine: the first visit: a Sikh kitchen where even an emperor sat on the floor
carry: seva: everyone eats at the same height
tomorrow: guided visits: what a Buddhist means by the breath
last: KARMA · BHAKTI · JNANA — ALL A DOING.

cards: Shoes off. Head covered. Hands washed.

You're in a gurdwara, a Sikh house of worship, and in the kitchen at the back someone is already handing you a plate. This week is different. Every other door on this app spent its first camp teaching its own first words.
Now you get to visit, one house a day. A guest has one simple rule: listen to how they say it, in their words, and don't take it home and blend it into yours.

teach.b: Sit down on the floor, in a row, next to whoever's there. This is the langar, the free kitchen, open to anyone of any faith or none.
Sikhs trace it to Guru Nanak, the first Guru, and they tell a story about the third, Guru Amar Das. He asked everyone who came to see him to eat in the langar first, in the same rows.
Then the emperor Akbar came to visit, the most powerful man in India. Tradition says there was no private table for him. He sat on the floor with everyone else, ate, and only then met the Guru.

Everyone at the same height. That's the first thing seva means in a Sikh home: service that erases rank, in a world where caste often decided who could eat beside whom. The second: it takes your whole self.

teach.h: BODY, MIND AND WHAT YOU HAVE.
teach.b: Sikhs speak of seva with the body, cooking, sweeping, minding the shoes; with the mind; and with what you have.
The third: it has no bill. In the Sukhmani, a long hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says, in effect, that the one who serves without wanting anything back reaches the Master.
For Sikhs, seva is remembering God with your hands. Now, from your own door. You met seva on day fifteen, and Hindu homes keep an old Sanskrit line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is God.
Feeding whoever comes isn't foreign to you. The honest difference: a Hindu host honors the guest as God; in the langar, the row itself is the teaching. Host, guest and emperor, one floor.

how: Sikhs do seva in the gurdwara by cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, sweeping, and caring for shoes, and outside it through relief work; the langar serves a free meal to anyone who comes, seated together on the floor.

o: a duty owed to a guru in return for blessing
volunteer hours logged to earn a good name
service given freely, with no reward expected

games.q: you're the emperor Akbar, arriving to meet Guru Amar Das. you're told to eat in the langar first. what do you do?
o: sit on the floor in the row and eat.
send your servants to eat for you.
games.why: tradition says Akbar sat on the floor with everyone else and ate. in the langar, even an emperor is at the same height.

practice: Bring to mind the next meal you'll share, at home, at school, at work. Picture everyone at it sitting in one row on one floor, nobody at the head of the table.
Then think of one plate you could hand to someone this week, with no bill attached. If you pray, you can offer the food first, the way many Hindu homes do.

wordCard.voice: Seva, selfless service, as Sikhs say it: a kitchen floor where everyone eats at the same height, with your whole self, and no bill attached.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for seva, selfless service, the first word of the Sikh door's camp one.

carryVoice: Your line: seva, everyone eats at the same height. Even an emperor sat on that floor. That's the first house.
